w: Giuseppe Pettazzi's 1938 petrol station spreads two 15-metre unsupported concrete wings like an aircraft caught mid-takeoff. City engineers, certain the cantilevers would collapse, demanded supporting pillars; legend says Pettazzi threatened to shoot himself if workers added them. They stand unpropped to this day.
s: A 1938 filling station shaped like a plane
why: One of the boldest unsupported concrete cantilevers of the pre-war futurist era, and the emblem of Asmara's UNESCO-listed modernist skyline.

n: Palace of Assembly, Chandigarh Capitol Complex
w: Le Corbusier crowned India's newest state capital with a raw-concrete legislature whose roof erupts in a chimney-like hyperbolic paraboloid, ventilating the chamber below like a cooling tower. Sun-breakers and a forecourt pool set the mood; the nearby Open Hand monument turns slowly in the wind as its symbol.
s: A concrete parliament with a cooling-tower roof
why: Centrepiece of Le Corbusier's UNESCO-listed Capitol Complex, among the most influential works of postwar concrete architecture.

w: Louis Kahn spent the last fourteen years of his life on this parliament house, a fortress of concrete and marble strips rising from an artificial lake, its geometric apertures cut like a keyhole into ancient forms. Construction outlasted a war and the birth of a nation; Kahn died before it was finished in 1982.
s: Louis Kahn's lakeside concrete parliament fortress
why: Widely regarded as Louis Kahn's masterpiece and one of the twentieth century's most significant government buildings.

w: Joze Plecnik clad his 1941 library in irregular blocks of rough and smooth stone, a deliberate patchwork meant to evoke a city rebuilt from rubble and knowledge assembled from fragments. Inside, a dim black staircase of rising columns forces visitors upward from darkness into the sunlit reading room above.
s: Plecnik's stone library, dark stair into bright hall
why: Plecnik's acknowledged masterwork and the symbolic heart of his UNESCO-listed remaking of Ljubljana.

w: MVRDV bent an entire apartment block into a horseshoe arch and hung a food hall beneath it, then wallpapered the 11,000-square-metre soffit with a fruit-and-flower fresco visible from every stall below. Two glass walls seal the ends, turning the whole market into the world's largest indoor artwork over groceries.
s: A horseshoe of flats arched over a food hall
why: One of the most photographed pieces of contemporary Dutch architecture, combining housing and market hall under a single painted vault.

w: Gerd Hanska's 1981 animal-testing laboratory for the Free University hunkers on stilts like a battleship run aground, its windowless flanks and rounded corners built to seal in noise and contamination. Locals nicknamed it the mouse bunker for its rodent labs; the profile still reads as pure Cold War fortress.
s: A windowless concrete lab shaped like a beached ship
why: One of Berlin's most extreme and photographed examples of West German institutional brutalism, now a protected monument.

w: William Pereira set a tiered glass crown on eight sculpted concrete legs so the upper floors appear to hover over the eucalyptus canyon below, an effect he compared to hands holding up a stack of books. Floor numbering skips level three entirely, feeding decades of campus rumours about a hidden secret floor.
s: A library that looks like hands holding books aloft
why: One of the most recognisable brutalist buildings in the United States, occupying a deliberate space between fortress and spaceship.

w: Completed in 1979 on land reclaimed from Table Bay, this striated concrete tower of ribbed columns and deep-set windows was designed to project municipal authority over the newly built Foreshore district. Its scale and severity made it an instant target for critics, and an equally instant icon of the skyline.
s: A ribbed concrete tower ruling the reclaimed Foreshore
why: One of Cape Town's tallest and most debated brutalist landmarks, symbolising the city's postwar civic ambitions.

w: David Mutiso and Karl Henrik Nostvik raised this 28-storey concrete cylinder in 1973 as the ruling party's new headquarters, its tapering ribs and rooftop helipad announcing an independent Kenya's arrival on the world stage. Climb the spiral ramp inside for one of the best panoramas over the whole city.
s: Nairobi's 1973 ribbed tower with a rooftop helipad
why: Kenya's most recognisable postcolonial landmark and an enduring symbol of independence-era optimism in concrete.

w: Built by Bulgarian contractors for the 1977 pan-African arts festival FESTAC, this vast saddle-roofed hall was modelled on a Nigerian military beret worn at a rakish tilt. Two swooping shells shelter theatres and conference halls beneath a single silhouette that still dominates the Lagos mainland skyline.
s: A 1977 concert hall shaped like a tilted beret
why: West Africa's most ambitious FESTAC-era building, its swept concrete roof one of the boldest civic silhouettes on the continent.

w: Tao Gofers stacked 79 public housing units into a jumble of interlocking concrete boxes in 1980, giving low-income tenants the same harbour views as the towers next door. A decade-long campaign, complete with a resident chained to her balcony, saved it from demolition before its 2018 conversion to private flats.
s: Stacked concrete boxes facing the harbour bridge
why: Australia's most fought-over brutalist building, saved from demolition after a public campaign over social housing and heritage.

w: Moshe Safdie was 29 and fresh out of a McGill thesis when Expo 67 let him build it for real: 354 prefabricated concrete boxes stacked and rotated into 146 homes, each with a private garden roof formed by the unit below. Inspired by Mediterranean hill towns, it promised suburban space at urban density.
s: 354 stacked concrete boxes from a student thesis
why: The single most famous built experiment in modular housing, and the only Expo 67 structure still used for its original purpose.

w: Luis Barragan, sculptor Mathias Goeritz and painter Jesus Reyes Ferreira set five hollow concrete triangles of differing heights and colour beside the motorway in 1957, meant to be read in motion by drivers speeding past. No plaques, no function, just abstract colour marking the threshold of a new suburb.
s: Five colour-block towers greeting drivers into the suburb
why: A landmark collaboration between Barragan and Goeritz that helped define postwar Mexican monumental sculpture and roadside architecture.

w: Corina Kavanagh, a wealthy spurned bride, reportedly commissioned this 1936 tower to block the view from the church where her ex-fiance's family worshipped. At 120 metres it was briefly the tallest reinforced-concrete building on earth, its stepped art deco profile still cutting a hard edge over Plaza San Martin.
s: A jilted heiress's spite tower over Plaza San Martin
why: South America's tallest building of its era and one of the finest examples of art deco skyscraper design outside the United States.

w: Georgi Stoilov's 1981 flying-saucer memorial to Bulgarian socialism crowns a 1,441-metre peak, its interior once lined with 500 square metres of glass mosaics and 35 tons of cobalt tesserae. Stripped and gutted since 1989, the concrete disc is now under restoration and visible from far down the mountain road.
s: A gutted concrete flying saucer on a Balkan peak
why: The most famous piece of socialist-era monumental brutalism in the Balkans, an unmistakable silhouette on the Bulgarian skyline.

w: Sculptor Vojin Bakic wrapped a 37-metre steel-panelled hull around a WWII partisan memorial in 1981, its mirrored curves designed to be seen glinting through the forest canopy from kilometres away. Stripped bare and abandoned after Yugoslavia's collapse, the exposed concrete skeleton still rises above the treeline.
s: A stripped steel-hulled memorial hidden in the forest
why: One of the most striking and remote of the Yugoslav 'spomenik' war memorials, an abstract sculptural landmark deep in the woods.

w: Kim Swoo-geun gave this 1981 church a fortress-like brick and concrete exterior with no obvious front door, forcing worshippers to circle the building before finding their way in, a deliberate pilgrimage before prayer. Inside, the sanctuary narrows upward like the hull of a ship turned toward the sky.
s: A brick fortress church with a hidden entrance
why: One of Kim Swoo-geun's most personal works and a landmark of Korean brutalist sacred architecture.

w: Design Partnership stepped this 1973 mixed-use tower back in a diagonal terrace so every flat and office kept its own open-air balcony, an early vision of a self-contained vertical city. Long dubbed 'Little Thailand' for its migrant-worker shops and remittance agents, it was formally conserved in 2021.
s: A terraced 1973 vertical city on Beach Road
why: Singapore's pioneering mixed-use brutalist megastructure, conserved as one of the country's defining modernist landmarks.

w: Louis Kahn spent over a decade shaping this business school campus from local brick, cutting vast circular and triangular openings into load-bearing walls to pull light and cross-breeze through un-air-conditioned dormitories and classrooms. Deep verandas and courtyards do the cooling that machines were never meant to.
s: Kahn's brick campus, cooled by geometry not machines
why: Widely ranked among Louis Kahn's finest works and a defining monument of postcolonial Indian institutional architecture.

w: A construction workers' cooperative raised this 39-storey Y-shaped tower in 28 months in 1956, briefly the world's largest reinforced-concrete building and Cuba's tallest for over sixty years. Revolution-era shortages left its rooftop restaurant and pool derelict, but the silhouette still commands Vedado.
s: A workers'-cooperative concrete tower over Vedado
why: The defining mid-century modernist skyscraper of pre-revolutionary Havana, built at record speed by its own future tenants.

w: Tomas Jose Sanabria perched this cylindrical 1956 hotel on the summit of a 2,159-metre peak above Caracas, reachable only by a cable car strung straight up the cloud forest. Decades of closure left it a ghostly landmark visible from the whole valley before a 2010s renovation reopened its panoramic dining room.
s: A cylindrical 1956 hotel on a cable-car summit
why: One of Latin America's boldest mid-century mountaintop hotels, reachable only by the cable car that made it possible.

w: Enver Hoxha's daughter and son-in-law designed this 1988 mausoleum-turned-museum as a glass pyramid to honour the dead dictator, its sloped white sides soon used as a slide by local children rather than a shrine. Left derelict for decades and covered in graffiti, it reopened in 2022 as a tech education centre.
s: A dictator's mausoleum, now a graffitied tech hub
why: Albania's most contested piece of architecture, transformed from communist mausoleum to public youth and tech centre.

n: Skopje Post Office and Telecommunications Centre
w: Janko Konstantinov shaped this 1974-81 complex like an unfurling lotus in raw concrete, its ribbed dome and asymmetric utility towers designed as part of Skopje's post-earthquake modernist rebuilding under Kenzo Tange's masterplan. A 2013 fire gutted the interior murals, but the sculptural exterior survives intact.
s: A concrete lotus rebuilt after Skopje's 1963 quake
why: One of the standout structures of Skopje's Kenzo Tange-guided reconstruction, and a landmark of Yugoslav brutalism.

w: Rebuilt after the 1931 earthquake flattened the city, this 1932 bank fuses stripped-classical art deco with carved Maori patterning, its zigzag mouldings echoing both traditions at once. A bronze grille above the entrance depicts Rumano the whale, one of the clearest fusions anywhere of deco form and Maori motif.
s: Art deco banking hall carved with Maori patterns
why: New Zealand's finest example of Maori motifs fused with art deco, built during Napier's famous post-earthquake reconstruction.

w: Henry Hohauser stacked a neon-lettered vertical sign atop this 1935 Ocean Drive hotel, its porthole windows, racing stripes and eyebrow overhangs distilling the nautical streamline moderne that defines South Beach. Restored in the 1980s preservation push, it remains one of the district's most photographed facades.
s: A neon-signed streamline hotel on Ocean Drive
why: One of the most photographed buildings in the Miami Beach Architectural District, the largest concentration of art deco in the world.

w: Kenzo Tange hung a suspension-bridge roof from a single central cable strung between two concrete pylons for the 1964 Olympics, giving the swimming hall a swooping, shell-like form with no interior columns to block a single seat's view. Half a century on, engineers still study its structural sleight of hand.
s: Tange's suspension-bridge roof over an Olympic pool
why: Widely regarded as one of the finest sports buildings ever built, and the structure that announced Kenzo Tange to the world.

w: Sumet Jumsai designed this 1986 bank headquarters as a literal robot, complete with bolt-eyes, antennae and tapering nut-shaped columns, a rebuttal to the postmodern classicism fashionable at the time. It celebrates the coming computerisation of banking, its steel eyelids even blinking with electric light.
s: A bank headquarters shaped like a giant robot
why: One of the most literal and beloved pieces of postmodern architecture in Southeast Asia, designed to celebrate the computer age.

w: Khalil Khoury drew this raw-concrete showroom and studio in 1973, but Lebanon's civil war halted work for over two decades before it was finally completed in 1996 to his original plans. Left to decay for years afterward, it was revived by his family in 2024 as a symbol of Beirut's fragile modernist heritage.
s: A 1973 concrete showroom finished after a war
why: One of the clearest surviving statements of Lebanese brutalism, recently revived as a landmark of the country's modern heritage.
